query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: Aluminum incorporation in CrFeCoNiX alloys drives the preferential formation of a slow‐growing, coherent Al2O3 scale, which offers exceptional oxidation protection above 900 °C by minimizing oxygen ingress and cation mobility.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single-phase metallic solid solution state.
generation.intervention: Replace X with Al, comparing the oxidation behavior against variants with Mn or Si under otherwise equivalent alloy compositions.
generation.conditions: Exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous and adherent Al2O3 layer forming at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum possesses a strong oxygen affinity and forms a highly stable, slowly growing alumina (Al2O3) film that acts as an effective barrier to both oxygen and cation diffusion. This minimizes volumetric expansion and stress accumulation, leading to improved scale adherence and durability compared to oxides formed from less reactive elements.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys containing Al will display a coherent and defect‐free Al2O3 scale with significantly reduced spallation and lower oxidation rates, unlike Mn- or Si-containing alloys which will form less protective oxides.
generation.baseline: Alloys where X is Mn or Si, which are anticipated to generate porous or non-adherent oxide scales under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: Applicable to both single‐ and multiphase high-entropy alloys exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in aggressive environments.
generation.uncertainty: While interactions with elements such as Cr, Fe, Co, and Ni may slightly modify kinetics, the fundamental alumina formation is dominant; however, quantitative effects of minor compositional variations remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Mn, or Si under identical processing. Expose all samples to high-temperature oxidation (>900 °C) and compare oxide layer morphology, adherence, and oxidation kinetics.
measurements: SEM/TEM to analyze oxide scale coherence and defect density.
XRD for phase identification (confirming Al2O3 presence in Al-alloys).
Thermogravimetric analysis to monitor oxidation rates and weight gain.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy fails to develop a significantly more coherent and protective oxide scale than the Mn- or Si-containing variants (i.e., if oxidation kinetics and spallation are similar), then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Chen et al. investigated the effect of Si (0.3 atom %) content on the oxidation behavior of the Al0.6CrFeCoNi HEA and found that the oxidation kinetics of the Si-containing HEA was lower than that of the Al0.6CrFeCoNi HEA at lower temperatures (800 and 900 °C) but became inferior compared to Al0.6CrFeCoNi at the higher temperature of 1000 °C. Lu et al. reported the effect of Al content on the oxidation behavior of Y/Hf-doped AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.7, 1, 1.3) high-entropy alloys. Al0.7CoCrFeNi showed the lowest oxidation resistance owing to the formation of an outer spinel layer with an inner Al2O3 layer, followed by AlCoCrFeNi due to the formation of protective Al2O3 scale and Al1.3CoCrFeNi exhibiting the highest resistance to oxidation. While the major focus of prior studies has been on the development of new alloy systems, there are only a few studies on limiting the high temperature oxidation via tailoring the material’s microstructure.
